newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan ruling party in N.Korea mission - papers.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan ruling party in N.Korea mission - papers.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party will send a large business delegation to North Korea to discuss direct air links and other investments, local newspapers said on Saturday.

Central Investment Co, one of the party's seven holding companies, was scheduled to lead the business mission to Pyongyang in May, the United Daily News quoted the company's chariman Yang Chung-tse as saying.

The Nationalist Party, one of the world's wealthiest political parties, would consider investing in hotel and textile businesses in North Korea if Taipei and Pyongyang establish air links, Yang was quoted as saying.
Taipei currently has no diplomatic ties with the North.

North Korea maintains formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan's arch rival, China, which has regarded the island as a renegade province since the Nationalist government lost a civil war to communist troops and fled to Taiwan in 1949.
The Nationalist Party has maintained close, but low-profile, contacts with the impoverished Stalinist state in recent years.

One of its firms, Yu Tai Co, has quietly conducted barter trade with several North Korean state enterprises, with Taiwan providing rice and soybeans in exchange for steel and aluminium, the daily said.

But such trade stopped in the end of 1996 when floods hit North Korea. Pyongyang then proposed to to let the Nationalists manage a 1,000-room hotel in order to repay some US$50 million debts, Yang told the paper.
Yang and other Nationalist officials were not available for comments.
Taiwan has made several moves to bolster unofficial ties with North Korea since South Korea, once its closest Asian ally, shocked Taipei by switching recognition to Beijing in 1992.
On Friday, Taiwan;s foreign ministry said it would send mid-ranking officials to North Korea to monitor Taiwan's shipments of humanitarian food aid to North Korea.

"We agreed last year to donate 2,000 tonnes of rice to North Korea and it should not be not surprising that we would send officials to monitor the rice shipment and delivery," a Taiwan foreign ministry official told Reuters.
The foreign ministry official said Taiwan's motive in helping North Korea reflected only humanitarian considerations and should not be interpreted as a bid to promote relations with Pyongyang.
Taiwan's Liberty Times quoted Foreign Minister John Chang as saying Taiwan had offered to send North Korea US$1 million in food aid and $1 million in cash.
A first shipment of rice and other food left Taichung Harbour in central Taiwan on March 28 and already had arrived in North Korea, the paper said.
Cash-strapped North Korea has been plagued by severe food shortages, with regular reports of imminent famine.
Local media reported that Pyongyang had acknowledged that at least 100 children had died of starvation.
North Korea defied Chinese protests to open a Taipei travel office in 1996 and has begun doing business with Taiwan.

Pyongyang agreed in January to accept up to 200,000 barrels of low-radiation nuclear waste from state-run Taiwan Power Co for disposal in North Korea in a deal reportedly worth US$230 million -- sparking protests from South Korea.
